title: why so many gods?
hook: why there are so many gods, and which one is yours

segments.voice: Yesterday: arti, light passed hand to hand. Today, the question every Hindu kid gets asked at school.

Someone at school or work asks it, half curious, half teasing: how many gods do you have? Ganesha on the dashboard, Krishna in the calendar, Durga at Navratri, Lakshmi at Diwali, a whole shelf at your grandparents' place. It's a fair question, and most people never got a good answer to give. Here's one. First, a guess.
screen: `HOW MANY GODS DO YOU HAVE?` → `A FAIR QUESTION.` → `HERE'S AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: One of the oldest Hindu verses says it in five words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. That line is how a lot of Hindus answer the question. The many gods are many faces and names of one reality, the way one person can be a mother, a boss and a friend and still be one person. Not every Hindu puts it the same way. Some families give their whole devotion to Vishnu, or Shiva, or the Goddess, and see the others as part of that one. Some honor many, each for a different part of life. Almost everyone has an ishta devata: a chosen deity, the form of God that feels like yours. Often it comes from your family. Sometimes you find your own. So the answer to the question at school can be simple: one truth, many names, and one of them feels like home.
screen: `TRUTH IS ONE.` · `THE WISE CALL IT BY MANY NAMES.` · `MANY FACES, ONE REALITY.` · `THE ONE THAT FEELS LIKE YOURS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of the image of God you saw most growing up: on a wall, a dashboard, a shelf. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say its name once, quietly, as if it were the name of someone who knows you.
Ishta devata. Your chosen deity: the form of God that feels like yours. Sixth word.
Your line: one truth, many names. Next time someone asks how many gods you have, you've got an answer. Day six.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep images of several deities; many families have a chosen deity (ishta devata) and a family deity, and devotion ranges from one god held as supreme to many honored together.

original.note: Sanskrit: ishta, chosen or dear, and devata, a deity. the form of God that's yours.

trapdoor: what you thought: a crowded shelf of separate gods.

what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.164.46, ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti; ishta-devata, the chosen deity of personal devotion, often alongside a family deity (kuladevata).

story.title: how many gods are there?
story.text: A student once kept pressing a famous teacher: how many gods are there? Three thousand and six, the teacher said. The student pushed. Thirty-three. Pushed again. Six. Three. Two. One and a half. Finally: one. Each time, the teacher showed how the bigger number folds into the smaller, until there was nothing left to fold.

notes: Editor pass (days 8–14): cut the superlative 'about as big as words get'; the teach's closing no longer has the narrator endorse the not-two reading right after saying nobody has to choose (the river image is now the Upanishad's, the wave framed as 'one way of hearing it'); practice's 'if you pray' line reworded.

Written from the camp-one manuscript day 11 under the claims rule: 'the single most famous sentence in the Upanishads, four words in Sanskrit' (the count and superlative), 'every tradition in the house has a version' and 'most people who grow up in the tradition hold it loosely' were cut.

The manuscript's ocean-and-wave image is kept as the title and closing line, and the textual image is the Chandogya's rivers reaching the sea (6.10) plus salt in water (6.13). Confirm both paraphrases.

Summaries of Advaita (not two), Vishishtadvaita (one whole with real differences; Brahman as inner ruler, antaryamin, of the self) and Dvaita (self and God distinct, the self dependent) need a Keeper's check for fairness.
Brahmin glossed as 'the priestly class'; confirm the phrasing (the manuscript said 'a caste').

Audit (2026-10-01): 'the river doesn't vanish into the sea, it arrives' was the narrator's gloss, not the text, and leaned toward one school; now says what Chandogya 6.10 says (the rivers become the sea). Salt (6.13), rivers (6.10) and tat tvam asi (6.8.7 to 6.16) references checked.
Editor review 2: 'Advaita reads it straight' implied the other Vedanta schools bend the text, a ranking a Vishishtadvaita or Dvaita reader would catch; now 'reads it as identity'.
